# Tricks from the BMS book {#sec-tricks}

The [Biologische Modellen en Statistiek](https://tbb.bio.uu.nl/bvd/bms/) book
(source in `Onderwijs/bms/Boek`) uses a handful of tricks that lift it above a
plain document. Each one below is pulled straight from that book's source so you
can copy it. None of them is hard — they are just not obvious from the getting-
started docs.

## Embedding interactive content with iframes

This is the flagship trick: dropping a live simulation right next to the text.
The book does it ~48 times. There are two flavours.

**A hosted applet** (a jsfiddle or a page on the UU server), embedded with a raw
HTML block so Quarto passes it through untouched:

```{.html}
<iframe id="iframeToReplace" width="100%" height="550"
        src="https://tbb.bio.uu.nl/bvd/bms/simulations/murmuraties/"
        title="Simulation"></iframe>
```

The `width="100%"` makes it responsive to the page width; `height` is fixed per
embed to suit the content (the book uses 330–680px depending on the applet). The
`id="iframeToReplace"` is not decorative — it hooks into the print script
(below).

**A self-contained HTML file that lives inside the project.** This is the
pattern for AI-generated single-file tools (see Rutger's example at the end).
From `Statistiek/Kansverdelingen.qmd`:

```{.html}
<iframe src="Applets/critical_value_calculator.html"
        width="100%" height="680"
        style="border:none; border-radius:10px; margin: 1em 0;">
</iframe>
```

The `src` is a *relative path* to an HTML file sitting in an `Applets/`
subfolder. Quarto copies it into the rendered site automatically. The inline
`style` (no border, rounded corners, vertical margin) is a nice touch that makes
an embedded tool look like a native part of the page.

## `freeze` and `cache`: two different re-rendering controls

These both stop Quarto re-running code unnecessarily, but they solve *different*
problems and live in different places. The BMS `_quarto.yml` sets both
explicitly, with helpful comments:

```yaml
execute:
  freeze: false  # auto -> re-render only when source changes
  cache: false   # true -> re-render chunks only when chunk changes
```

The difference, which is worth teaching clearly:

**`freeze`** operates at the *file* level and is about *portability*. With
`freeze: auto`, Quarto runs a chapter's code once, stores the results in a
`_freeze/` folder (which you commit to Git), and afterwards reuses them until
the `.qmd` source changes. The payoff: a colleague — or a CI server — can render
the whole book *without* having R/Python and every package installed, because
the computed results travel with the repo. The BMS repo has a `_freeze/` folder
for exactly this. `freeze: true` never re-runs; `freeze: false` (his current
setting) always runs fresh.

**`cache`** operates at the *chunk* level and is about *speed during authoring*.
It uses knitr's cache (or Jupyter's) to skip re-running an individual code chunk
whose code hasn't changed, so a slow simulation doesn't re-run every preview.
The caches live in per-chapter `*_cache/` folders (you can see them under
`Statistiek/StatistiekRutger/`).

Rule of thumb to pass on: **`cache` for "this chunk is slow while I write",
`freeze` for "others should be able to build this without my setup".** They can
be combined, and both can be overridden per-file or per-chunk.

## Sharing LaTeX macros between HTML and PDF

The book defines its maths shorthand once and uses it in both outputs. The
macros live in `_macros.tex`, e.g.:

```tex
\providecommand{\dd}{\mathrm{d}}
\providecommand{\deriv}[3][]{\frac{\diff^{#1}#2}{\diff #3^{#1}}}
\newcommand{\dt}[1]{\frac{\mathrm{d}#1}{\mathrm{d}t}}
\providecommand{\ev}[1]{\mathbb{E}\!\left[#1\right]}
\providecommand{\var}[1]{\mathrm{Var}\!\left(#1\right)}
```

Every chapter that needs them starts with a Quarto *include shortcode* on the
very first line:

```markdown
{{{< include ../_macros.tex >}}}
```

Because the file contains `\newcommand` / `\providecommand` definitions, they
are picked up by **MathJax** in the HTML output and by **LaTeX** in the PDF — so
`$\dt{N}$` renders correctly in both from a single definition. Using
`\providecommand` (rather than `\newcommand`) for most of them is deliberate: it
avoids "command already defined" clashes if a macro name overlaps with something
LaTeX already knows.

*Note:* `_macros.tex` also has a few `\usepackage{...}` lines (e.g. `xcolor`)
that only apply to the PDF build; MathJax simply ignores those, which is why the
same include is safe for both.

## Custom SCSS theming

The book's `stylesheet` uses Quarto's SCSS structure — a `defaults` block for
variables and a `rules` block for CSS:

```scss
/*-- scss:defaults --*/
$primary:  #e8601d !default;   // UU-ish orange accent
$font-size-root: 18px !default;

/*-- scss:rules --*/
body { line-height: 1.6; }
img  { width: 80%; }
figcaption { max-width: 75%; margin: 0 auto; }  // centre captions
```

It also defines `.print-only` / `.screen-only` helper classes wrapped in an
`@media print { … }` block, so some elements only appear on screen and others
only on paper — see the print section below.

## Callouts and cross-references

Two more pedagogy-friendly features used throughout. Callouts for tips/warnings:

```markdown
::: {.callout-important appearance="default" icon=false}
Key result: the critical value depends on both $\alpha$ and df.
:::
```

And auto-numbered cross-references — label a figure with `#fig-cover` (or a
section with `#sec-odes`) and refer to it with `@fig-cover` / `@sec-odes`. Quarto
numbers them and makes them clickable, and the numbers stay correct when you
reorder chapters.

## Is `print_friendly.html` still used? (short answer: no)

**What it was.** `print_friendly.html` was *not* a Quarto format or extension —
it was Bram's own little `<script>` that made the browser's "Print → Save as
PDF" produce a clean result. On `window.onbeforeprint` it swapped every
`<iframe id="iframeToReplace">` for a placeholder linking to the live version
(you can't print an interactive iframe), and restored the page afterwards. The
surviving copy is at `bms/Boek/scripts/print_friendly.html`:

```html
<script>
  window.onbeforeprint = () => {
    const iframes = document.querySelectorAll("iframe#iframeToReplace");
    iframes.forEach((iframe, index) => {
        const placeholder = document.createElement('div');
        placeholder.innerHTML += "<br><center><font size=1><i>Deze interactieve "
          + "content vind je <a href='" + iframe.src + "'>hier</a>...</i></font></center>";
        iframe.parentNode.replaceChild(placeholder, iframe);
    });
  };
  window.onafterprint = () => { window.location.reload(true); };
</script>
```

It used to be wired into chapters with `{{{< include ../print_friendly.html >}}}`.

**Is it deprecated?** In his current book, effectively yes — he has already
moved on. The file no longer exists at the project root, and there is **no live
`.qmd` that includes it** (the only remaining references are stale entries in
RStudio's search-history cache under `.Rproj.user/`). The only copy left is the
unused one in `scripts/`. So the book currently ships **without** the print
script; its print handling now rests on the CSS `@media print` rules and the
`.print-only` / `.screen-only` classes in the stylesheet.

**Recommendation.** Don't teach the JS-include approach as a pattern — it's a
clever hack from before Quarto had good native tools, and it's brittle (relies
on a magic id, reloads the page after printing). For new books, prefer:

- **Conditional content** for "show a static fallback in print/PDF, the live
  thing on the web". This is the native, supported mechanism:

  ```markdown
  ::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
  <iframe src="Applets/critical_value_calculator.html" width="100%" height="680"></iframe>
  :::

  ::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
  ![Critical-value calculator (interactive version online)](figuren/calc_screenshot.png)
  :::
  ```

  (Caveat: conditional content is applied *after* computation, so a chunk that
  emits HTML-only output should also be gated with a chunk option like
  `#| eval: !expr knitr::is_html_output()`.)

- A **real `format: pdf`** target for a proper printable book, which he is
  already halfway to since `_macros.tex` supplies the LaTeX side. That is far
  more robust than "print from the browser". Typst (`format: typst`) is a
  lighter-weight modern alternative if a full LaTeX toolchain is a hassle.

In short: `print_friendly.html` is retired in his build, and the modern
replacement is `content-visible when-format` plus a native PDF/Typst format —
no custom print script needed.

## Worked example: embedding Rutger's self-contained applet

Rutger's tool is a good real-world example of "an AI-style single-file HTML app
dropped into a Quarto book". The file is:

```
bms/Boek/Statistiek/Applets/critical_value_calculator.html
```

Its `<title>` is literally **"Rekenhulp: Bereken de kritieke waarde"**. It is a
single self-contained file (~770 lines: inline CSS and JavaScript, with one
external CDN `<script>` for Chart.js) — exactly the kind of artefact an AI
coding tool produces.

To reuse this pattern in a new book, the whole recipe is two steps:

**1. Put the HTML file in a subfolder of your project**, e.g. `Applets/`, next
to the chapter that uses it. Quarto treats it as a project resource and copies
it into the rendered site.

**2. Embed it with a relative-path iframe** in a raw-HTML block — the exact
block Bram uses:

````markdown
Je kunt de kritieke waarde die hoort bij een waarde van $\alpha$ berekenen
met de applet hieronder.

```{=html}
<iframe src="Applets/critical_value_calculator.html"
        width="100%" height="680"
        style="border:none; border-radius:10px; margin: 1em 0;">
</iframe>
```
````

Tips to pass on: keep the applet **self-contained** (inline everything, or use
CDN links) so there are no broken relative paths after rendering; set `height`
to fit the tool (this one needs ~680px); use `width="100%"` for responsiveness;
and, if you also produce a PDF, wrap the iframe in a
`::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}` block with a screenshot fallback for
print (see the print section above).
